title: C Program Structure and Syntax
learningObjectives: Explain the purpose and role of c program structure and syntax in a C program.
Identify the relevant C language constructs, standard-library facilities or toolchain responsibilities.
Read a focused example and explain its data flow and control flow.
Recognize common errors, portability concerns and safety considerations for this topic.
Apply the concept in a small C program and verify it with compiler diagnostics and tests.

understand.concept: A C program is made from declarations, function definitions, statements, expressions and preprocessing directives. The compiler parses these constructs according to the language grammar. Braces delimit compound statements and function bodies; semicolons terminate many declarations and expression statements; identifiers name program entities.
understand.whyItMatters: Understanding the structure of a C translation unit helps you read compiler diagnostics, organize functions and avoid common syntax errors. It also prepares you to separate declarations in header files from definitions in source files.
understand.analogy: Think of a C program as a set of precise instructions that must be translated for a particular machine and execution environment.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy does not replace the formal C language rules, object lifetimes, types or implementation-defined behaviour.

explain.narrative:
A common beginner program includes a standard header, defines main, places statements inside braces and returns an integer status. The preprocessor handles directives such as #include before the compiler parses the resulting translation unit. A directive begins with # and is not terminated by a semicolon.

C is case-sensitive: `total`, `Total` and `TOTAL` are different identifiers. Keywords such as int and return have reserved meanings and cannot be used as ordinary identifiers. Names must follow identifier rules and should communicate purpose.

Whitespace and line breaks usually separate tokens but do not define the program's block structure; braces do. A missing semicolon, unmatched brace, misspelled identifier or misplaced declaration can cause a diagnostic at a later line than the original mistake. Read the first relevant diagnostic and inspect the preceding code.

examples.title: Identify the main parts
examples.explanation: The directive includes declarations for printf. The function definition begins with a return type and parameter list. Braces delimit its body; declarations and statements appear inside.

examples.title: Case-sensitive identifiers
examples.code: int total = 12;\nint Total = 20;\nint difference = Total - total;
examples.explanation: The identifiers total and Total are distinct. Consistent naming avoids accidental confusion.

practise.guidedTask: Annotate a short C program by identifying its preprocessing directives, function declaration, parameter list, compound statement, local variable, function call and return statement.
practise.independentTask: Write a two-function program and intentionally introduce a missing semicolon, mismatched brace and misspelled variable. Fix each compiler diagnostic and explain why the parser may report a later location.
hints: A preprocessing directive starts with # and is processed before ordinary compilation.
Many declarations and expression statements end with semicolons.
Fix the earliest meaningful compiler error first; later errors may be consequences.
